title: Semicolons: Joining Two Complete Sentences
kicker: American Diploma · Digital SAT · Grammar: Boundaries
summary: When a semicolon is allowed (two independent clauses, and the SAT/ACT list rule), how it works with however and therefore, and every place it is wrong — with 10 practice questions.

blocks.text: What this question type tests

Semicolon questions are part of the **Boundaries** skill in the **Standard English Conventions** domain (about 26% of the scored Reading and Writing questions, 11–15 questions). The skill covers punctuation that links clauses and separates list items — and the semicolon does both. It is also one of the favorite **wrong** answers: test writers put it in the choices because it looks “advanced.”

You get a short passage (25–150 words) with a blank and the stem **“Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?”** Typical choices: “rock, it” / “rock; it” / “rock it” / “rock; and it.” You must know exactly when a semicolon is allowed — and it is allowed in only **two** situations.

blocks.title: الفاصلة المنقوطة = نقطة
blocks.text: الفاصلة المنقوطة (;) شغلتها الأساسية إنها توصل بين جملتين كاملتين بينهم علاقة. الاختبار السهل: لو ينفع تحط نقطة (.) مكانها والجزئين يفضلوا جمل كاملة، يبقى الفاصلة المنقوطة صح. لو أي جزء مش جملة كاملة، يبقى غلط.
Rule 1: A semicolon joins two independent clauses
**The teacher's rule:** a semicolon joins **two independent clauses** (two complete sentences) that are closely related. Both sides must be able to stand alone as sentences.
**The period test:** replace the semicolon with a period. If both parts are still complete sentences, the semicolon is correct. If either part becomes a fragment, the semicolon is wrong.

items: ✓ Marble is a metamorphic rock; it forms when limestone is exposed to great heat and pressure.
✓ Some desert plants store water in their thick leaves; others store it in underground stems.
✓ The museum was full by ten o'clock; visitors had been waiting since dawn.
✓ The experiment failed twice; the third attempt succeeded.
✗ Because the road was closed; the bus took a longer route. (left side is a dependent clause)
✗ The volunteers worked through the night; because the water was rising. (right side is a dependent clause)
✗ The team collected samples from forty sites; making it the largest survey of its kind. (right side is a phrase)
✗ The tour visited three cities; Luxor, Aswan, and Cairo. (right side is a list, not a clause — use a colon)

blocks.title: Watch for hidden subjects
blocks.text: A clause that starts with a pronoun is still independent: “it forms …,” “others store …,” “this means …,” “they left …”. These pronoun starts are where comma splices hide, and a semicolon fixes them.
Rule 2: Semicolon + conjunctive adverb

Words like **however, therefore, as a result, for example, in fact, instead, consequently, moreover, meanwhile** are not FANBOYS. They cannot join two clauses with only a comma. When one of them begins the second independent clause, use a **semicolon before** it and a **comma after** it (or a period).

items: ✓ The bridge was too narrow for modern trucks; therefore, the city built a wider one beside it.
✓ The bridge was too narrow for modern trucks. Therefore, the city built a wider one.
✗ The bridge was too narrow for modern trucks, therefore, the city built a wider one. (comma splice)
✗ The bridge was too narrow for modern trucks therefore, the city built a wider one. (run-on)

blocks.text: **But** when the adverb sits **inside** one clause, it is an interrupter and takes a pair of commas — no semicolon: “The second trial, however, was cancelled.” To decide, check what comes **before** the adverb: a complete sentence (→ semicolon) or just a subject (→ commas).

items: ✓ The first trial was a success; however, the second was cancelled. (complete sentence before “however”)
✓ The second trial, however, was cancelled. (only the subject before “however”)
✗ The second trial; however, was cancelled. (“The second trial” is not a sentence)

blocks.text: Rule 3: No semicolon with FANBOYS between two clauses
A semicolon already does the joining. When you join two independent clauses with **for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so**, the test's standard choice is a **comma** before the FANBOYS word.

items: ✓ The road was closed, and the bus took a longer route.
✓ The road was closed; the bus took a longer route.
✗ The road was closed; and the bus took a longer route. (choose “, and” or “;” — not both)

blocks.text: Rule 4: The places a semicolon can never go

rows: after an introductory dependent clause or phrase
Although the bridge was finished in May; it did not open until October.
before a dependent clause (because, which, although, when, who …)
The team won; because it trained harder.
before a phrase or a list that is not a clause
The kit had three tools; a compass, a whistle, and a lamp.
Many dishes; such as koshari and ful, use beans.
between a subject and its verb, or a verb and its object
The students in the club; built a robot.
inside a clause before an interrupter
The final results; however, were different.

blocks.title: SAT/ACT extra rule — semicolons in a complicated list
items: This is an exam rule for the SAT and the ACT. It is the ONLY other use of the semicolon you need for these tests.
When the items in a list **already contain commas**, use semicolons between the items, so the reader can see where each item ends.
✓ The tour visits three cities: Luxor, Egypt; Amman, Jordan; and Tunis, Tunisia.
✓ The panel included Dr. Salma Adel, a geologist; Dr. Youssef Amin, a chemist; and Dr. Rana Farid, an engineer.
✗ The tour visits three cities: Luxor, Egypt, Amman, Jordan, and Tunis, Tunisia. (How many cities? It is impossible to tell.)
Be consistent: if one break between items is a semicolon, every break between items is a semicolon — including before the final “and.” The commas INSIDE each item stay commas.
This is the one case where “; and” is correct.

blocks.text: Semicolon or something else? Comparing the marks

rows: a colon (list/explanation) or a single dash (emphasis)

blocks.text: **A semicolon does not change the meaning.** It only shows that two complete, related sentences are joined. The relationship between them — addition, result, example, or difference — comes from the **words** (however, therefore, for example, instead), never from the semicolon itself. So when you choose a semicolon, ask a grammar question (complete + complete?), not a meaning question.

**If two choices both look correct** — for example a period and a semicolon in the same place — they cannot both be the key. Look for a second difference: a missing comma after “however,” an extra “and,” or a word that turns a clause into a fragment.

blocks.title: قاعدة القوائم (خاصة بـ SAT و ACT)
blocks.text: لو كل عنصر في القائمة جواه فاصلة (زي Luxor, Egypt أو Dr. Salma Adel, a geologist)، نفصل بين العناصر بـ ; ونخلي الفواصل اللي جوه العنصر زي ما هي. ولازم نكون ثابتين: كل الفواصل بين العناصر تبقى ; حتى اللي قبل and الأخيرة.
Worked examples
**Worked example 1 — two independent clauses**

Text: Plants that live in very dry places have developed different ways of surviving long periods without rain. Some desert plants store water in their thick, fleshy leaves ______ store it in large underground stems that stay cool below the sand.
**Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?**

items: A) leaves, others
B) leaves; others
C) leaves others
D) leaves: others,

blocks.text: **Answer: B**

items: A) ✗ Wrong: Both sides are independent clauses (“others store it …” is complete), so a comma alone makes a comma splice.
B) ✓ Correct: A semicolon joins two closely related independent clauses. Period test: “Some desert plants store water in their thick, fleshy leaves. Others store it …” ✓
C) ✗ Wrong: No punctuation between two independent clauses is a run-on.
D) ✗ Wrong: The comma after “others” separates the subject from its verb “store.”

blocks.text: **Worked example 2 — conjunctive adverb**
Text: The old iron bridge over the canal was built for horse carts, not heavy vehicles. It was too narrow for modern trucks ______ the city built a wider bridge beside it in 2010.
**Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?**

items: A) , therefore,
B) ; therefore,
C) therefore
D) , therefore

blocks.text: **Answer: B**

items: A) ✗ Wrong: “Therefore” is not a FANBOYS word, so a comma before it creates a comma splice.
B) ✓ Correct: “It was too narrow for modern trucks” and “the city built …” are both complete; a semicolon before “therefore” and a comma after it is the standard pattern.
C) ✗ Wrong: With no punctuation, two independent clauses run together.
D) ✗ Wrong: Comma splice, and the comma after “therefore” is missing too.

blocks.text: **Worked example 3 — SAT/ACT extra rule**

Text: An international conference for young scientists is held in a different city every year. Over the next three years, the conference will visit Luxor, Egypt ______ Amman, Jordan; and Tunis, Tunisia.
**Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?**

items: A) Egypt,
B) Egypt:
C) Egypt
D) Egypt;

blocks.text: **Answer: D**

items: A) ✗ Wrong: Each item already contains a comma (“Luxor, Egypt”), and the text later uses “Jordan; and,” so this break must also be a semicolon. A comma makes the list confusing and inconsistent.
B) ✗ Wrong: A colon cannot be placed in the middle of a list.
C) ✗ Wrong: With no mark, “Egypt Amman” runs two items together.
D) ✓ Correct: Semicolons separate list items that contain commas, and this choice is consistent with “Jordan; and Tunis.”

blocks.text: **Worked example 4 — when the semicolon is the trap**
Text: Scientists recorded water temperatures every week for ten years. They collected samples from forty different sites along the coast ______ the largest survey of its kind in the region.
**Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?**

items: A) coast; making it
B) coast, making it
C) coast. Making it
D) coast; and making it

blocks.text: **Answer: B**

items: A) ✗ Wrong: The right side (“making it the largest survey …”) is a participle phrase, not a clause, so a semicolon is wrong.
B) ✓ Correct: A comma attaches the participle phrase to the complete sentence before it.
C) ✗ Wrong: The period leaves “Making it the largest survey of its kind in the region.” as a fragment.
D) ✗ Wrong: A semicolon + “and” before a phrase: two errors.

blocks.title: Classic traps
items: **Semicolon after an introduction:** “Although …; it …”.
**Semicolon before a dependent clause or phrase:** “; because …”, “; which …”, “; making …”, “; such as …”.
**Semicolon before a list:** “three tools; a compass …” — a list after a complete sentence needs a colon.
**Semicolon + FANBOYS** between two clauses: “; and the …” (only correct in the SAT/ACT list rule).
**Comma splice with however/therefore:** “…, however, the …” between two complete sentences.
**Inconsistent list:** semicolons between some items and commas between others.
**Thinking a semicolon carries meaning:** it never “shows” anything; the words do.

blocks.title: Fast strategy for test day
items: Do the period test: could a period go where the semicolon is, with complete sentences on both sides? Yes → semicolon allowed. No → cross it out.
Before however/therefore: complete sentence on the left → “; however,”. Only a subject → “, however,”.
See commas inside list items? Use semicolons between all the items.
If a period and a semicolon both seem right, find the second difference in the choices.

blocks.text: Practice
Ten original Digital SAT-style questions. Do the period test on every semicolon you see.

blocks.title: Semicolons — Practice Quiz
blocks.intro: 10 questions · untimed. Before choosing a semicolon, check that both sides are complete sentences — or that you have a list whose items contain commas.

questions.p: Many famous buildings, from the Taj Mahal to ancient Roman temples, are made of the same beautiful stone. Marble is a metamorphic rock ______ forms when limestone is exposed to great heat and pressure deep underground.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: Both sides are independent clauses, and the semicolon joins them. A is a comma splice, C is a run-on, and D uses a semicolon together with “and.”

questions.p: Coins appeared in Egypt only late in its ancient history. For most of the pharaonic period, the ancient Egyptians did not use coins at all ______ they traded goods directly or measured value in weights of copper and grain.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: “Instead” begins the second independent clause, so it needs a semicolon before it and a comma after it. A and B are comma splices; C is a run-on.

questions.p: A new national program will fund research on water use in agriculture. The selection panel included Dr. Salma Adel, a geologist ______ Dr. Youssef Amin, a chemist; and Dr. Rana Farid, an engineer who designs irrigation systems.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: SAT/ACT extra rule: the list items already contain commas, and the text uses a semicolon later (“chemist; and”), so every break between items must be a semicolon. B is confusing and inconsistent; C puts a colon inside a list; D runs two items together.

questions.p: Heavy rain upstream caused the river to rise very quickly on Thursday evening. In a small village near the river, volunteers filled sandbags and worked through the night ______ the flood water had reached the edge of the village.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: “Because the flood water had reached …” is a dependent clause, so it attaches to the main clause with no punctuation. A semicolon (A) and a colon (B) cannot come before a dependent clause, and D leaves “Because …” as a fragment.

questions.p: Building the new bridge took longer than the engineers had planned. Although the bridge was finished in May ______ did not open to traffic until October, after months of safety tests.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: An introductory dependent clause (“Although …”) is followed by a comma. A and B need a complete sentence before the mark, and C leaves “Although the bridge was finished in May.” as a fragment.

questions.p: The museum's collection begins with objects from the earliest farming villages in Egypt. Its oldest object is a small clay jar ______ more than six thousand years old.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: “More than six thousand years old” is a phrase that adds information about the jar, so a comma attaches it. A, B and D all put a semicolon before a phrase that is not an independent clause.

questions.p: In 1783, two French brothers tested a large hot-air balloon in front of a crowd at the palace of Versailles. It was the first balloon flight to carry living passengers ______ passengers were a sheep, a duck, and a rooster.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: Both sides are independent clauses, so a semicolon joins them. B is a comma splice, C is a run-on, and D adds a wrong comma after “and.”

questions.p: The engineers ran two trials of the new irrigation pump in the desert. The first trial was a complete success. The second trial ______ was cancelled because of a sandstorm.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: “However” interrupts the clause “The second trial was cancelled,” so it takes a pair of commas. A, C and D use a semicolon, but “The second trial” is not a complete sentence.

questions.p: A travel company has planned a three-week river tour for next winter. The boat will stop in Aswan, Egypt; Wadi Halfa, Sudan ______ Khartoum, Sudan.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: SAT/ACT extra rule: the items contain commas, and the first break is already a semicolon, so the break before the last item must be “; and.” A is inconsistent, B puts a colon inside a list, and D runs the items together.

questions.p: The hiking club gives every new member a small emergency kit. The kit contains three tools ______ a compass, a whistle, and a flashlight.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: A complete sentence that promises “three tools” is followed by the list, so a colon is correct. A puts a semicolon before a list (not a clause), B is a comma splice, and C has no mark to introduce the list.

blocks.title: Remember
items: A semicolon joins two closely related complete sentences — the period test.
SAT/ACT extra rule: semicolons separate list items that already contain commas; be consistent, including “; and” before the last item.
“; however,” between two sentences; “, however,” inside one sentence.
Never before a dependent clause, a phrase, a list or examples; never after an introduction.
A semicolon never shows meaning by itself; the words do.
